Senses.PreferredTarget: revile the buddhas and curse the patriarchs
AlternateTargets: scold the buddhas and abuse the patriarchs
Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “scold or shout down” (呵, also written 訶), “buddhas” (佛), “curse or revile” (罵), and “patriarchs” (祖): "revile the buddhas and curse the patriarchs." Zen-scoped the string (呵佛罵祖) occurs 232 times across 118 texts; the graphic variants (訶佛罵祖) (33 hits / 24 texts), (呵佛叱祖) (4 hits, all the 楊岐 line below) and the inverted (罵祖呵佛) (2) also occur. Attested deployment: (1) as an epithet for a master's conduct — most often (德山)'s: (上堂德山呵佛罵祖承其言者多見德山者少) (a 上堂 of 真淨克文 in 古尊宿語錄), and paired with (臨濟)'s shout in another of the same master's (上堂) — (德山呵佛罵祖臨濟喝) (the same passage carried in both the C- and D-canon editions of 古尊宿語錄); (2) spoken in a master's own record of himself — (楊岐一語)。(呵佛叱祖)。(明眼人前)。(不得錯舉) (楊岐方會's record); (3) as an answer to a question — to "what is the shortcut teaching gate?" (如何是徑截法門) a master answers (訶佛罵祖去), and to "what is host-within-host?" (如何是主中主) another answers (訶佛罵祖); (4) as a conduct-label for a master — (和尚終日訶佛罵祖) (spoken by an attendant to the dying 真點胸), and (據猊床)，(而訶佛罵祖) (of a master on the lion-seat); (5) in a letter of (玉林通琇) — "that we could not, in the days when venerables stood thick as forests, go off to a solitary peak, tie together a grass hut, and revile the buddhas and curse the patriarchs — but instead prop up the tottering great house with chicken-rib strength, sorting demons and rebutting the different — is truly a great misfortune" (我輩不能于尊宿林林之日向孤峰絕頂蟠結草庵呵佛罵祖去迺以鷄肋之力撑持大廈之危辯魔斥異誠大不幸). The corpus also records a reply that glosses it: to "who is one who reviles buddhas and curses patriarchs?" (訶佛罵祖是甚麼人) a master answers "an icchantika" (闡提漢). The texts set the phrase beside "sort demons and screen the different" (辨魔揀異): (辨魔揀異)，(須是頂門具眼)；(訶佛罵祖)，(還他腦後見腮) (2 texts). The texts assign the phrase no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense; the four graphs are stable, and the variants (訶/呵, 叱/罵, inverted 罵祖呵佛 2, 罵佛呵祖 1) are grep-verified; (訶佛叱祖) and (呵佛喝祖) do not occur. Attribution: (楊岐方會) speaks the (呵佛叱祖) line in his own record (袁州楊岐山普通禪院會和尚語錄, T47n1994A). The two (德山)-epithet passages are (上堂) of (真淨克文) (雲庵真淨禪師語錄, inside the 古尊宿語錄 compilation; 德山宣鑒 is the SUBJECT, not the speaker). The B27n0152 letter passage is (玉林通琇)'s own reply (its duplicate at 0656a20 opens 師復書云); the correspondent's incoming letter is the inline (附原書) note. The J-canon answers (徑截法門, 主中主, 闡提漢) are from Ming/Qing (語錄) whose masters — (大溈五峰學) (Wufeng Ruxue), (蓮月), (三山燈來) — are not on the roster, so MasterName null; do NOT read the Tang roster master (五峰) into (大溈五峰學). Multi-source: T, C, B, D and J canons, multiple independent texts and masters.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'laugh loudly, ha-ha.' The phrase occurs 1,508 times in 278 allowlisted texts and is written into public encounters as an audible action, sometimes followed by speech and sometimes serving as the whole recorded response. The records preserve its range without assigning one fixed interpretation to it. Baizhang laughs after a colleague asks why he had just cried, and answers only, 'Just now I cried; now I laugh.' Zhaozhou laughs during an exchange and then repeats the other speaker's cry, 'Heaven! Heaven!' Jinniu dances with the rice tub, laughs loudly, and calls the assembly to eat. Another monk reports returning to eat after hearing the meal drum, whereupon the master laughs. A discourse can even laugh and then ask, 'Laugh at what?' The deviation lies in its textual role: laughter is preserved as a speaker-turn and public-interview action, not reduced to an editorial note about emotion.
Senses.Note: Different occasions do not establish different things. The phrase consistently denotes the audible act of laughing; the texts do not authorize a menu of motives.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, dust and toil. The compound occurs 1,353 times in 275 allowlisted texts and names the wear, bustle, and entanglement of ordinary affairs and responsive thought. Texts speak of worldly toil being unbroken, worldly affairs becoming empty, turning one's head within worldly toil, and having no worldly toil to avoid. One letter answers a complaint about the toil and commotion of the world by asking, 'Who is the worldly toil, and who is the one rejecting it?' A later address explicitly calls a quiet, easeful condition only a temporary rest from worldly toil and warns against recognizing it as final. Another discourse pairs being in dust and leaving dust, then says to leave the world in the midst of worldly toil.
Senses.Note: The frequent longer string 'worldly toil and vexation' occurs 36 times in 24 texts, but the entry preserves the headword's own concrete dust-and-labor wording. Formula searches found no stable bare self-definition; the apparent 'worldly toil is ...' strings mostly introduce a person located amid it.

AlternateTargets: mote after mote, land after land
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “every mote and every land”: the repeated nouns make the phrase distributive. Across 205 occurrences in 116 allowlisted texts, Chan masters pair it with “each thing and each particular” (物物頭頭), say that every mote and land “fully displays” (全彰), and place it in public addresses as the range of an action or disclosure. One address says, “every mote and every land once manifested awe-inspiring light; each thing and each particular fully displayed the true eye” (塵塵剎剎，曾現威光。物物頭頭，全彰正眼). Another gives the compact parallel, “each thing and each particular—the whole body; every mote and every land—the great function” (物物頭頭全身，塵塵剎剎大用). The phrase is also made a test: “if you understand, every mote and every land; if you do not, a kick to the head” (若也會得，塵塵剎剎；若也不會，當頭一蹋). The corpus thus bends a cosmological distributive into recurring teaching-seat language for an all-pervading range; this entry makes no claim beyond those deployments.
Senses.Note: No second referent was found. Reversal as “land after land, mote after mote” (剎剎塵塵) changes order, not the thing denoted.
